case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may recognize (or should categorically refuse to recognize) aiding-and-abetting liability under the judicially inferred cause of action associated with the Alien Tort Statute and under the Torture Victim Protection Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Alien Tort Statute (ATS), 28 U.S.C. § 1350; Torture Victim Protection Act of 1991 (TVPA), 28 U.S.C. § 1350 note.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Cisco and related defendants) argue that federal courts should not extend ATS litigation to aiding-and-abetting (and potentially other secondary-liability) theories because doing so entails an improper, separation-of-powers-significant judicial creation/expansion of private causes of action in a domain that carries acute foreign-relations sensitivities. They contend that under Sosa’s framework—especially its second, discretionary step—courts should decline to recognize aiding-and-abetting claims given: (1) the modern Court’s strong reluctance to create implied causes of action; (2) the practical and diplomatic costs of forcing U.S. courts to adjudicate the legality of foreign officials’ conduct in their own territory; (3) the Court’s trend toward categorical limiting rules in ATS cases (e.g., extraterritoriality and corporate liability); and (4) the presumption associated with Central Bank of Denver that civil aiding-and-abetting liability is not available absent clear legislative authorization, which Petitioners say also informs the scope of TVPA liability.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Doe plaintiffs) argue that Sosa left the ATS ‘door not closed’ and permits federal courts to entertain tort suits by aliens for violations of the law of nations, not limited to the three paradigmatic 1789 offenses (safe-conduct violations, infringement of ambassadors’ rights, and piracy). On their view, aiding-and-abetting is not a wholly new cause of action but an accepted way of defining who may be held responsible for established international-law violations, and historical materials (including references to Blackstone-era understandings) support that secondary liability for core international-law offenses was contemplated. They maintain that Congress has not withdrawn that judicial role since 1789, and that recognizing aiding-and-abetting liability is consistent with the ATS’s text authorizing tort actions for violations of the law of nations and with Sosa’s recognition of limited, carefully cabined federal-court authority in this area.
key_precedents: Kiobel v. Royal Dutch Petroleum Co.
Central Bank of Denver, N.A. v. First Interstate Bank of Denver, N.A.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s reliance on Sosa footnote 20 is the strongest pushback: if “who may be liable” is part of a norm’s scope, aiding-and-abetting can look like application rather than innovation. But as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito emphasize, that same footnote underscores that international law rarely supplies remedial machinery, so recognizing secondary civil liability is ultimately a domestic-law choice—precisely where Sosa step two demands special caution and where our trajectory in Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé favors categorical limiting principles to protect institutional legitimacy and avoid foreign-relations friction. Justice Sotomayor’s proposed mens rea/substantial-assistance filters are sensible as policy, but they do not cure the separation-of-powers problem that Central Bank highlights: absent clear congressional authorization, we should not presume implied civil aiding-and-abetting in this sensitive domain, and the TVPA’s “subjects” text is not a clear statement. A narrow holding—no ATS aiding-and-abetting (and no TVPA secondary liability) absent explicit statutory direction—best fits our post-Sosa restraint and leaves any expansion to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—reading Sosa footnote 20 to treat aiding-and-abetting as part of a norm’s “scope of liability” rather than a new cause of action—still does not solve the threshold problem that the ATS is jurisdictional and any civil liability rule (especially secondary liability) is domestic remedial machinery that international law does not itself supply. As Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, footnote 20 cuts against respondents by confirming that courts would be making a distinctly policy-laden choice, triggering Sosa’s step-two separation-of-powers caution. In that setting, Central Bank’s reluctance to infer implied civil aiding-and-abetting absent clear authorization is an appropriate interpretive baseline, and the TVPA’s “subjects” language is not a sufficiently clear textual instruction to expand liability in this foreign-relations-sensitive, judge-made regime. Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, reflect our trajectory toward categorical limiting principles to avoid diplomatic friction, not further judicial elaboration of liability doctrines.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is that aiding-and-abetting is merely a “mode of liability” that can be treated as part of defining the scope of an accepted law-of-nations norm, with Sosa footnote 20 inviting consideration of “who may be liable.” But footnote 20 also underscores that international law does not supply the remedial machinery, leaving federal courts to make domestic policy choices—exactly where Sosa’s step-two “special caution” and our post-Sosa decisions (as Chief Justice Roberts stresses) counsel categorical restraint rather than further judge-made elaboration in a foreign-relations minefield. Central Bank is therefore not a stray analogy; it supplies the interpretive default that we do not presume civil aiding-and-abetting absent clear authorization, and neither the ATS’s jurisdictional text nor the TVPA’s “subjects” language speaks with the clarity needed to overcome that default. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s workability proposals (mens rea/substantial assistance filters) are policy responses that do not answer the separation-of-powers problem: deciding whether to expose secondary actors to this diplomatically fraught litigation is for Congress, not us.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Central Bank-based institutional-restraint argument is the strongest on the other side, but it does not carry the same force where Sosa (including footnote 20) explicitly contemplates limited federal common-law development of “who may be liable” once a universally accepted norm is identified. Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito are right that international law often does not supply “remedial machinery,” yet that is precisely why Sosa directs courts to apply familiar liability principles cautiously rather than to impose a categorical immunity that would predictably shield knowing, substantial facilitators of torture. Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé, as Roberts and Barrett stress, tighten gatekeeping (extraterritoriality, proper defendants, domestic conduct), but they do not compel an across-the-board rejection of secondary liability in paradigmatic, universally condemned abuses; those doctrines can manage foreign-relations risk without creating an accountability gap. On the TVPA, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Barrett’s narrow reading of “subjects,” because ordinary usage allows one to “subject” a victim to torture through direction or substantial assistance, and Congress’s remedial aim is undermined if we exclude purposeful enablers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the Central Bank-style interpretive default: absent clear congressional authorization, we should hesitate to imply civil aiding-and-abetting in a foreign-relations minefield. But that default cannot do the work they assign it here, because Sosa itself (including footnote 20) tells courts that once an accepted international-law norm is identified, we must still determine the norm’s “scope of liability,” i.e., who can be held responsible—so recognizing aiding-and-abetting in that limited, norm-anchored way is not the freewheeling creation of a new regime. Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé, as Roberts and Barrett emphasize, reinforce caution, but they function mainly as gatekeeping constraints (presumption against extraterritoriality, proper defendants, and domestic conduct) rather than mandates for categorical immunity for knowing, substantial facilitators of universally condemned violations. On the TVPA, I agree with Justice Sotomayor that “subjects” is naturally read to include those who knowingly and substantially enable torture under color of law, and I do not see enough textual basis to treat Congress as silently excluding familiar secondary-liability principles in a statute designed to ensure accountability.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is her Sosa footnote 20 argument that aiding-and-abetting can be treated as a “mode of liability” within the norm’s “scope of liability,” rather than a new ATS cause of action. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, footnote 20 also recognizes that international law rarely supplies the remedial machinery, so extending judge-made ATS/TVPA remedies to secondary civil liability is a domestic-law choice triggering Sosa step-two’s special-factors restraint and separation-of-powers concerns. Justice Sotomayor’s proposal to manage risk through mens rea and substantial-assistance filters is a policy calibration, not an answer to whether courts have authority to create that additional layer of liability in this foreign-relations-sensitive domain. Central Bank’s no-presumption rule against implied civil aiding-and-abetting, pressed by Justice Alito, supplies the proper interpretive default absent a clear congressional statement, and neither the ATS’s jurisdictional text nor the TVPA’s “subjects” language provides one.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Sosa footnote 20 treats aiding-and-abetting as part of a norm’s “scope of liability” rather than a new ATS cause of action—still does not solve the step-two problem: footnote 20 simultaneously recognizes that international law generally does not supply remedial machinery, so adopting secondary civil liability is a domestic, judge-made choice. Given Sosa’s “vigilant doorkeeping,” and our legitimacy/foreign-relations trajectory in Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé (as the Chief Justice emphasizes), I think a categorical refusal to extend ATS/TVPA to aiding-and-abetting absent clear congressional instruction is the more institutionally sound rule. Justice Alito’s Central Bank analogy is persuasive as an interpretive backdrop: when the underlying cause of action is already implied and fraught with diplomatic consequences, we should be especially reluctant to infer additional layers of civil liability from silence or ambiguous terms like the TVPA’s “subjects.” The respondents’ proposed mens rea/substantial-assistance filters (Justice Jackson) are policy calibrations, but they do not supply the clear authorization that my methodology requires before expanding judge-made liability in this domain.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is her Sosa footnote 20 framing: that aiding-and-abetting can be treated as part of the accepted norm’s “scope of liability” rather than a new norm. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the same footnote underscores that international law “does not supply the remedial machinery,” so recognizing secondary civil liability is still a domestically chosen extension of a judge-made cause of action—precisely where Sosa’s step-two special-factors analysis and our caution in Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé counsel restraint. Justice Sotomayor’s reading of the TVPA’s “subjects” to include facilitators is plausible, but under a textualist approach the term does not clearly codify accomplice liability, and ambiguity is not enough when the decision would meaningfully expand exposure in a foreign-relations-sensitive domain. Central Bank does not control, but (as Justice Alito notes) it captures the interpretive reluctance to imply civil aiding-and-abetting absent clear authorization—a reluctance at its apex when courts are already operating at the edge of their lawmaking competence under the ATS/TVPA framework.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that, under Sosa step two and our cautions in Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé, adding civil aiding-and-abetting risks impermissible judge-made expansion in a foreign-relations minefield, with Central Bank supplying a background presumption against implying secondary liability from silence. But that argument treats Central Bank as a near-categorical bar even though it arose in a very different, congressionally detailed securities scheme, whereas Sosa footnote 20 (as Justice Kagan emphasizes) directs a norm-by-norm inquiry into the “scope of liability,” including “who may be liable,” once a universally accepted violation is identified. The post-Sosa cases can do their intended gatekeeping work—limiting extraterritorial reach, proper defendants, and domestic conduct—without creating an across-the-board immunity for knowing, substantial facilitators of paradigmatic abuses like torture; demanding mens rea/substantial-assistance thresholds (as Justice Sotomayor urges) are not freewheeling policymaking but practical tailoring to avoid systemic diplomatic friction while preserving accountability. Because my approach is pragmatic and fairness-focused, I do not find the separation-of-powers concerns sufficient to justify a categorical rule that predictably leaves victims without a remedy against purposeful enablers where the underlying norm is already settled and the case can be cabined by existing doctrines.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, recognizing new ATS causes of action (and the contours of any implied remedy) requires “vigilant doorkeeping,” including a discretionary step attentive to separation-of-powers and foreign-relations consequences; extending that judge-made remedy to aiding-and-abetting liability would be a significant further step better left to Congress. Our subsequent ATS cases—Kiobel (presumption against extraterritoriality), Jesner (refusing to extend ATS to foreign corporate defendants), and Nestlé (requiring domestic conduct tied to the focus of the statute)—reflect a consistent move toward narrowing, categorical limits to protect institutional legitimacy and avoid diplomatic friction. Sosa’s footnote 20 suggests that questions of who may be liable are not dictated solely by international law and may require domestic-law judgments; in domestic law, Central Bank of Denver counsels strongly against implying civil aiding-and-abetting absent clear legislative authorization, which likewise points against reading the ATS or the TVPA to encompass such secondary liability.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Alien Tort Statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is purely jurisdictional and does not itself create a cause of action; under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, any judicially inferred remedy must be tightly confined and recognized only with “great caution,” particularly given separation-of-powers and foreign-relations concerns. Extending that already-inferred remedy to aiding-and-abetting would further expand federal common law beyond the statute’s original public meaning and beyond the “modest number” of paradigmatic 1789 offenses Sosa described, and this Court’s later ATS decisions (e.g., Kiobel and Jesner) underscore the need for categorical limits rather than further judicial innovation. For the TVPA, Congress specified liability for an “individual” who subjects another to torture or extrajudicial killing, and absent clear statutory text authorizing secondary civil liability, the presumption reflected in Central Bank of Denver counsels against recognizing aiding-and-abetting as an implied theory. Whether to authorize such secondary liability in these sensitive domains is for Congress, not the federal courts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The ATS is a jurisdictional provision, and under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain any judicially inferred cause of action must be narrowly cabined, with special hesitation where foreign-relations consequences are substantial; recognizing aiding-and-abetting would materially expand ATS litigation beyond what Congress authorized. Central Bank of Denver holds there is no general presumption of civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear statutory authorization, and neither the ATS, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, nor the TVPA, 28 U.S.C. § 1350 note, contains such an authorization. Our more recent ATS decisions (Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé) repeatedly stress restraint and categorical limiting rules to avoid the practical costs and diplomatic friction of U.S. courts adjudicating foreign conduct. In that context, the prudent course—consistent with separation of powers and Congress’s role in this sensitive area—is to refuse to recognize aiding-and-abetting liability under the ATS and to reject it under the TVPA as well.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS remains available for a narrow class of well-defined, universally accepted international-law violations, and Footnote 20 recognizes that federal courts may look to domestic common-law principles to shape the remedial contours of the judicially inferred action—including questions of who may be held liable. Aiding-and-abetting is best understood not as a new ATS “cause of action,” but as a standard mode of assigning responsibility for established violations of the law of nations; a categorical bar would unduly insulate those who knowingly facilitate torture or other grave abuses, undermining fairness and access to justice for vulnerable victims. Kiobel and Jesner counsel caution about extraterritoriality and certain defendants (e.g., foreign corporations), but they do not compel a blanket rule eliminating secondary liability across the board, particularly where plaintiffs allege purposeful assistance to international-law violations. The TVPA, which creates an express cause of action for torture and extrajudicial killing, likewise should not be read to foreclose aiding-and-abetting categorically when that mode of liability is consistent with the statute’s remedial purpose and established accountability norms.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS permits a narrowly cabined federal common-law cause of action for well-defined, universally accepted international-law norms, and footnote 20 indicates that courts look to international law to determine the “scope of liability” for a norm—an inquiry that can include whether accomplice (aiding-and-abetting) responsibility is part of the international-law definition of the offense. A categorical bar on aiding-and-abetting liability would be in tension with that Sosa framework and with the ATS’s text authorizing suits for any “tort ... committed in violation of the law of nations,” 28 U.S.C. § 1350, because it would artificially narrow who may be held responsible for an established violation rather than policing the norm’s definiteness and the case’s foreign-relations sensitivity at Sosa’s step two. By contrast, the TVPA is an express statutory cause of action, and its text reaches any individual who “subjects” a person to torture or extrajudicial killing, which can naturally encompass directing or knowingly assisting such acts, without importing Central Bank’s securities-specific presumption to override ordinary interpretive tools. Workability and coherence are best served by allowing aiding-and-abetting where international law (for ATS) or statutory text (for TVPA) supports it, while using Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé to keep the ATS limited through other constraints (e.g., extraterritoriality and separation-of-powers caution) rather than a blanket rule.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The ATS is “strictly jurisdictional,” and any judicially inferred cause of action under it must remain narrowly cabined under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain; recognizing civil aiding-and-abetting liability would be an additional, separation-of-powers-significant step with acute foreign-relations consequences that the Judiciary is ill-suited to undertake, as Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé underscore through their repeated insistence on caution and limiting rules in ATS litigation. Independent of the ATS, the TVPA’s text creates liability for an individual who, “under actual or apparent authority, or color of law,” subjects a person to torture or extrajudicial killing, and it says nothing about secondary liability; under Central Bank of Denver, there is no general presumption of civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear statutory authorization. Where Congress has not spoken clearly—and where extending liability risks embroiling courts in sensitive foreign-policy judgments—the better course is to leave any expansion to Congress, not to judicial implication. At a minimum, any ambiguity about expanding a judicially inferred remedy in this domain should be resolved against expansion, consistent with Sosa’s second-step caution and the separation of powers.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, recognizing new features of ATS litigation requires “vigilant doorkeeping,” and the Court’s later ATS decisions (Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé) have repeatedly adopted limiting rules in light of foreign-relations sensitivities and separation-of-powers concerns. Aiding-and-abetting liability would significantly expand the judicially inferred ATS cause of action beyond the narrow set of historically grounded claims Sosa contemplated, and it would create serious practical and diplomatic burdens by drawing U.S. courts into disputes over foreign conduct. For the TVPA, the text creates an express cause of action against an individual who “subjects” another to torture or extrajudicial killing, and in light of Central Bank of Denver’s strong presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear congressional authorization, I would not read secondary liability into that language. Congress knows how to provide aiding-and-abetting liability expressly, and in this sensitive area it is Congress—not federal courts—that should decide whether to extend civil liability to secondary actors.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The ATS is a jurisdictional statute, and under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain federal courts may recognize only a “modest” set of law-of-nations claims while exercising great caution at Sosa’s discretionary step two—especially where foreign-relations consequences and separation-of-powers concerns are acute. Recognizing aiding-and-abetting as a freestanding civil theory under a judicially inferred ATS cause of action would expand judge-made liability in a domain where this Court has increasingly adopted limiting principles (Kiobel’s extraterritoriality limits, Jesner’s rejection of corporate liability, and Nestlé’s insistence on domestic conduct). For the TVPA, the statute creates an express cause of action against an “individual” who “subjects” a person to torture or killing, and absent clear textual authorization for secondary liability, Central Bank of Denver’s presumption against implied civil aiding-and-abetting liability counsels against reading it in. In short, methodological consistency with our implied-cause-of-action jurisprudence and the ATS line of cases requires declining to recognize aiding-and-abetting liability here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS permits a “limited” federal common-law cause of action for well-defined, universally accepted international-law norms, and Footnote 20 indicates courts should consider not just the norm but the appropriate scope of liability for actors connected to that norm. Aiding-and-abetting is best understood as a mode of responsibility tied to an established law-of-nations violation (step one), with step two’s cautionary, pragmatic inquiry reserved for case-specific separation-of-powers and foreign-relations concerns rather than a categorical bar. A categorical refusal to recognize any secondary liability would unduly narrow § 1350’s authorization of tort actions for violations of the law of nations and would also be difficult to square with the TVPA’s remedial purpose to provide a civil remedy for torture and extrajudicial killing (28 U.S.C. § 1350 note), particularly where procedural fairness counsels against immunizing knowing facilitators. Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé counsel restraint (especially where U.S. conduct is thin or foreign-relations concerns are acute), but they do not require an across-the-board elimination of aiding-and-abetting when plaintiffs plausibly allege substantial assistance to universally condemned violations and when courts can manage practical consequences through rigorous pleading, causation, and mens rea requirements.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may recognize aiding-and-abetting liability (and potentially other forms of secondary liability) in suits brought under the Alien Tort Statute’s judicially implied cause of action and/or under the Torture Victim Protection Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1350 (Alien Tort Statute); Torture Victim Protection Act of 1991 (TVPA), Pub. L. No. 102-256, 106 Stat. 73 (codified as note to 28 U.S.C. § 1350).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Cisco argues that recognizing civil aiding-and-abetting liability under the ATS would be an improper judicial expansion of a judge-made cause of action that this Court has repeatedly instructed lower courts to treat with exceptional caution. Petitioners emphasize separation-of-powers limits (courts should not create new forms of ATS liability), foreign-relations sensitivities (aiding-and-abetting claims often require U.S. courts to pass on the legality of foreign sovereign conduct abroad), and the presumption against civil aiding-and-abetting liability drawn from Central Bank of Denver (absent a clear congressional directive). They also suggest that, even if framed as a mere ‘scope’ question rather than a new cause of action, the same Sosa step-two discretion/guardrails counsel against recognizing such secondary-liability theories, potentially extending to conspiracy as well.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend that Sosa left the door open for federal courts to adjudicate a narrow set of modern law-of-nations torts and that aiding-and-abetting is not a forbidden ‘new cause of action’ but a conventional means of enforcing established international-law norms by reaching facilitators, not just principal perpetrators. They argue the ATS text broadly covers torts committed in violation of the law of nations (not merely the three historical paradigms like piracy), and that historical materials (including references to Blackstone and the founding-era understanding) support the availability of liability for those who assist core international-law violations. Respondents further stress that Congress has not withdrawn ATS adjudicatory authority since 1789, and they resist categorical limits that would foreclose case-by-case adjudication under Sosa.
key_precedents: Kiobel v. Royal Dutch Petroleum Co. (2013)
Central Bank of Denver, N.A. v. First Interstate Bank of Denver, N.A. (1994)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that Sosa footnote 20 contemplates consulting international law on the “scope of liability,” and that accessory concepts are a familiar incident of responsibility. But under Sosa’s step-two “special hesitation,” we should treat the recognition of an ATS cause of action and the further decision to extend it to secondary actors as distinct, sequential exercises of judge-made power—Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé caution against that second enlargement given predictable foreign-relations consequences. Justice Thomas’s framing is persuasive for minimalist purposes: respondents have not identified a specific, universal, and obligatory international-law norm that clearly supports a U.S. civil damages action for aiding-and-abetting, as opposed to accessory liability in particular criminal contexts. Central Bank’s presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting, while arising in domestic statutes, still supplies a baseline restraint that applies with added force where §1350 is jurisdictional and any remedy is already implied, making a narrow holding declining to recognize ATS/TVPA aiding-and-abetting the most institutionally legitimate course.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is her reading of Sosa footnote 20 as a direction to look to international law for the “scope of liability,” but that footnote is best understood as a constraint: the norm itself must be specific as to who may be held liable, not an invitation to graft broad domestic secondary-liability doctrines onto a jurisdictional statute. Justice Jackson’s characterization of aiding-and-abetting as mere remedial “gap-filling” does not solve the separation-of-powers problem because it still enlarges a judicially implied ATS action in a way Sosa’s “special hesitation” and Kiobel/Jesner/Nestlé warn courts to avoid, especially given the foreign-relations consequences. Chief Justice Roberts’s point that importing civil aiding-and-abetting would be an additional, distinct step beyond recognizing any ATS claim is persuasive under a textualist framework: neither the ATS nor the TVPA clearly authorizes that step, and Central Bank’s presumption against implied civil aiding-and-abetting reinforces restraint where Congress has not spoken. Respondents have not identified a specific, universal, and obligatory international-law norm extending civil accessory liability to this defendant class, so I would not recognize it by judicial implication.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Sosa’s footnote 20 speaks of consulting international law on the “scope of liability,” and she (with Justice Jackson) treats aiding-and-abetting as a routine incident rather than a new cause of action. But read in context, footnote 20 reinforces Sosa’s core constraint: the norm must be specific not only as to primary conduct but also as to who may be held liable, and respondents have not identified a universally accepted, clearly defined international-law norm requiring civil aiding-and-abetting liability as opposed to accessory concepts in particular criminal tribunals. Even if one could characterize this as “remedial gap-filling,” as Justice Jackson urges, it would still be a major step-two policy choice that predictably expands ATS exposure with foreign-relations consequences—exactly what Kiobel and Jesner caution courts to avoid absent congressional authorization. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Central Bank’s presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting from silence applies with special force here because we would be enlarging a judge-made remedy atop a jurisdictional statute (and likewise stretching the TVPA’s carefully drafted text).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is that recognizing aiding-and-abetting risks a second-layer judicial enlargement on top of an already implied ATS action, and that Central Bank counsels against implying civil secondary liability from silence. But Central Bank’s presumption grew out of construing detailed domestic remedial statutes; by contrast, Sosa expressly contemplates a narrow federal-common-law cause of action keyed to international-law norms, and Footnote 20 directs us to consult international law on the “scope of liability,” where accessory responsibility is a familiar incident of universally condemned violations even if not labeled “civil” in the same way. Justice Kagan’s reading of Footnote 20 as a constraint is right as far as it goes, but it does not compel a categorical bar: we can require purposeful, knowing, and substantial assistance with a strong U.S.-conduct nexus (consistent with Kiobel/Nestlé) without immunizing facilitators as a class. Under my pragmatic approach, an across-the-board refusal to recognize any secondary liability would create predictable remedial gaps for grave abuses and undermine the ATS’s limited function where primary perpetrators are unreachable, while careful limits can address the foreign-relations concerns my colleagues raise.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that Sosa’s Footnote 20 contemplates consulting international law for “scope of liability” and permits some remedial gap-filling, so a categorical bar could create practical under-enforcement. But I read Footnote 20 as a limiting instruction: the norm must be specific not only as to the primary conduct but also as to the liability we are asked to recognize, and respondents have not shown a sufficiently definite, universally accepted norm that civil damages may be imposed on aiders and abettors as such. Even if one frames aiding-and-abetting as an “incident” rather than a new cause of action, adopting it still requires a consequential federal common-law choice to expand the class of defendants, and Kiobel/Jesner/Nestlé’s foreign-relations caution combined with Central Bank’s warning against implying civil secondary liability from silence counsels against courts making that choice—especially for the TVPA’s carefully drawn text. So I remain persuaded, consistent with the Chief Justice’s minimalism, that the most coherent and workable line is to decline recognizing aiding-and-abetting under both schemes and leave any expansion to Congress.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that Sosa’s footnote 20 contemplates consulting international law on the “scope of liability,” and that accessory concepts appear in some international materials. But under Sosa’s own framework, that consultation is a constraint, not a license: respondents must identify a specific, universal, and obligatory norm that extends liability to the defendant class, and the record does not establish a clearly defined customary international-law norm of civil secondary liability that would justify grafting a freestanding aiding-and-abetting regime onto a judicially implied ATS cause of action. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, recognizing aiding-and-abetting here would be “step two” enlargement of a judge-made remedy atop a jurisdictional statute, exactly the kind of move Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé warn carries foreign-relations and separation-of-powers costs best left to Congress. Central Bank’s caution against implying civil aiding-and-abetting from silence is not displaced by the ATS context; if anything, the absence of text is more consequential where the cause of action is already judicially created, and the TVPA’s careful enactment without express secondary liability confirms we should not supply it by judicial implication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Sosa’s Footnote 20 tells us to consider “the scope of liability,” and she argues that customary international law commonly includes secondary responsibility. But I agree with the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan that Footnote 20 operates as a constraint: it requires that any extension of liability be tied to a specific, universally accepted norm with defined contours, not a general invitation for us to graft a freestanding civil aiding-and-abetting regime onto an already judge-made ATS cause of action. Justice Jackson’s “gap-filling” framing does not overcome the institutional concern that Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé repeatedly emphasize—expanding ATS liability (especially in ways that predictably increase foreign-relations friction) is a policy choice better left to Congress. And for the TVPA, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, Central Bank’s presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting is especially forceful where Congress enacted a detailed cause of action and did not clearly authorize secondary liability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Sosa’s Footnote 20 asks courts to consider the “scope of liability,” which could be read to encompass some form of accessory responsibility. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Footnote 20 functions as a constraint—requiring the plaintiff to identify a specific, universal, and obligatory norm that itself supports the liability being asserted—rather than a license to graft a generalized domestic aiding-and-abetting regime onto a judge-made ATS cause of action. Justice Jackson’s “gap-filling” framing does not overcome Central Bank’s presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting from silence, and that caution applies with even greater force where §1350 is jurisdictional and Sosa already requires “special hesitation,” reinforced by Kiobel and Jesner’s foreign-relations concerns. On the TVPA, I remain unpersuaded that “subjects” or “[a]n individual” supplies the clear textual hook needed to infer secondary liability in a carefully drawn statutory cause of action.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the institutional one: that recognizing civil aiding-and-abetting could look like an additional layer of judge-made expansion atop a judge-made ATS remedy, with foreign-relations costs, and they invoke Central Bank’s presumption against implied secondary liability. But I remain unpersuaded that Central Bank controls in this setting, because it arose from interpreting a detailed congressional cause of action, whereas Sosa (including Footnote 20) contemplates limited federal-common-law implementation once a sufficiently definite law-of-nations norm is identified, and familiar accessory principles can function as a limiting doctrine rather than an open-ended enlargement. Justice Thomas’s insistence that plaintiffs must identify a “specific, universal, and obligatory” international-law norm of civil aiding-and-abetting liability reads Footnote 20 too rigidly; international law often defines the primary prohibition while leaving the incidents of responsibility (including facilitation) to be operationalized, subject to Sosa step-two caution and the domestic-conduct limits emphasized in Kiobel and Nestlé. As a practical matter, a categorical bar would create arbitrary remedial gaps for purposeful domestic facilitation of universally condemned abuses, and I do not read our precedents as compelling that across-the-board outcome.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS supports only a “very limited” set of judge-recognized claims grounded in norms that are “specific, universal, and obligatory,” and the Court has repeatedly cautioned against expanding this judicially implied cause of action absent clear congressional direction. Recognizing civil aiding-and-abetting liability would extend ATS litigation in a way that amplifies the foreign-relations and separation-of-powers concerns emphasized in Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé, particularly where the alleged assistance and underlying conduct occur abroad. Moreover, consistent with Central Bank of Denver’s presumption that Congress does not create civil aiding-and-abetting liability without speaking clearly, neither 28 U.S.C. § 1350 nor the TVPA supplies the textual hook to add secondary-liability doctrines by judicial implication. A narrow ruling declining to recognize aiding-and-abetting (and leaving other secondary-liability theories for Congress) best preserves institutional legitimacy and adheres to this Court’s modern ATS precedents.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Alien Tort Statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is jurisdictional text and does not itself authorize courts to create new forms of civil liability; under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain (2004), any judge-made ATS cause of action must be confined and developed with exceptional caution, leaving expansion to Congress. Recognizing aiding-and-abetting (and similar secondary-liability theories) would be a further judicial extension of an implied remedy, raising separation-of-powers and foreign-relations concerns emphasized in Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé. Moreover, absent a clear statutory directive, there is no general presumption of civil aiding-and-abetting liability, as Central Bank of Denver teaches, and neither the ATS nor the TVPA expressly supplies such secondary liability. Footnote 20 of Sosa reinforces that the relevant norm must extend liability to the particular defendant being sued, and respondents have not shown a universally accepted, specifically defined international-law norm of civil aiding-and-abetting liability that satisfies Sosa’s requirements.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The ATS, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is jurisdictional, and any cause of action under it is judicially implied and therefore must be kept on a very tight leash under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, especially where expanding liability would have substantial foreign-relations and separation-of-powers consequences, as emphasized in Kiobel and Jesner. Recognizing aiding-and-abetting (and potentially conspiracy) would be a significant enlargement of that judge-made remedy, not something the statute’s text affirmatively authorizes, and this Court has repeatedly warned against such expansions in ATS litigation. Central Bank of Denver counsels against implying civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear congressional authorization, and that caution applies with even greater force where the underlying ATS cause of action itself is judge-made. The TVPA’s text imposes liability on one who “subjects” an individual to torture, and absent an express secondary-liability provision Congress included elsewhere in federal law, I would not read that language to create aiding-and-abetting liability by implication.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS permits a narrow federal common-law cause of action for well-defined, universally accepted law-of-nations norms, and Footnote 20 instructs courts to look to international law to determine “the scope of liability for a violation of a given norm,” which supports recognizing conventional forms of secondary liability like aiding-and-abetting where customary international law treats facilitation as culpable. Cisco’s reliance on Central Bank of Denver is misplaced in the ATS context because ATS claims are not creatures of a detailed domestic statutory remedial scheme where Congress’s silence on aiding-and-abetting is dispositive; rather, the ATS incorporates international-law norms and their accepted incidents, subject to Sosa’s caution and Kiobel’s presumption against extraterritoriality as limiting principles. Foreclosing aiding-and-abetting categorically would unduly narrow the remedial purpose of the ATS/TVPA regime and risk denying any meaningful avenue of redress for victims of grave abuses who can rarely reach the principal perpetrators, contrary to Congress’s accountability aims in the TVPA and the ATS’s historic role in providing a forum for serious international-law violations. Concerns about foreign relations can be managed through Sosa’s step-two prudential restraint and case-specific analysis rather than an across-the-board bar on secondary liability.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS supplies jurisdiction and any cause of action is a restrained, judge-made federal common-law remedy subject to “step two” caution, particularly where recognizing a new liability theory risks foreign-relations friction and separation-of-powers concerns. Extending that implied ATS cause of action to aiding-and-abetting would be an additional federal common-law choice about the scope of liability that Congress has not authorized, and Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé underscore the Court’s reluctance to expand ATS litigation in ways likely to provoke international discord. For the TVPA, Congress created a specific statutory cause of action for torture and extrajudicial killing, and absent a clear textual directive authorizing secondary liability, Central Bank of Denver counsels against presuming civil aiding-and-abetting liability. A categorical refusal to recognize aiding-and-abetting under these schemes is the most workable and administrable line consistent with the Court’s modern ATS precedent and statutory coherence between ATS and the TVPA.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The ATS, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is jurisdictional and any cause of action under it is judicially implied and therefore must be kept on a “tight leash,” with special caution before extending it into new domains. Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, courts may at most recognize a narrow class of claims defined with specificity and restraint, and decisions like Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé reinforce that separation-of-powers and foreign-relations concerns counsel against judicially expanding ATS liability beyond what is clearly established. Recognizing civil aiding-and-abetting (or conspiracy) would be a further, judge-made enlargement of a judge-made remedy, and Central Bank of Denver’s presumption against civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear congressional authorization underscores that such an expansion should come from Congress, not courts. The TVPA, unlike the ATS, is statutory; its text does not expressly provide secondary liability, and absent a clear directive we should not read it to create aiding-and-abetting liability by analogy.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS is a jurisdictional statute and any judge-made cause of action must be tightly cabined, with “vigilant doorkeeping” and special hesitation where foreign-relations and separation-of-powers concerns are implicated. Recognizing civil aiding-and-abetting (and similar secondary-liability theories) as part of that implied ATS action would materially expand ATS litigation beyond what this Court has permitted in Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé, all of which underscore that further extensions of ATS liability are for Congress, not the Judiciary, especially given the foreign-policy sensitivities inherent in such suits. For the TVPA, Congress created a specific cause of action with defined defendants and remedies, and under Central Bank of Denver’s presumption against implied civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent a clear statutory directive, courts should not add secondary liability onto the TVPA’s text. Practical workability and the Court’s institutional role likewise counsel against opening a broad new avenue for ATS/TVPA suits based on attenuated facilitation theories.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The ATS, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is jurisdictional and the cause of action it supports is judicially implied and therefore must be tightly cabined under Sosa’s “vigilant doorkeeping,” including step two’s instruction that courts should hesitate absent clear authorization from the political branches. Recognizing aiding-and-abetting (and similar secondary-liability theories) would expand the scope of that judge-made remedy in a way this Court has repeatedly cautioned against in the ATS context, particularly given the foreign-relations and separation-of-powers concerns emphasized in Kiobel and Jesner. Sosa’s footnote 20 does not supply a free-standing license to import domestic secondary-liability doctrines; rather, it underscores that the inquiry must remain anchored in a specific, universally accepted norm and in careful judicial discretion, and this Court has never approved such an extension. For the TVPA, Congress created an express cause of action and specified who is liable (“[a]n individual”), and absent an explicit statutory directive, the presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting liability articulated in Central Bank counsels against reading secondary liability into the statute.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, 542 U.S. 692 (2004), once a plaintiff pleads a sufficiently definite and universally accepted law-of-nations norm, the remaining question is the proper scope of the judicially implied remedy; Sosa’s Footnote 20 contemplates looking to domestic-law principles in shaping that remedy, which supports recognizing familiar secondary-liability doctrines like aiding-and-abetting rather than treating them as a brand-new cause of action. Central Bank of Denver’s presumption against implied civil aiding-and-abetting liability is tied to statutory interpretation of particular congressional enactments, but the ATS cause of action is judge-made and historically aimed at providing a workable forum for law-of-nations violations, making common-law gap-filling more appropriate (subject to Sosa’s caution). Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé counsel restraint—especially given foreign-relations and extraterritoriality concerns—but they do not categorically foreclose secondary liability where plaintiffs allege domestic, purposeful facilitation of universally condemned conduct; a categorical bar would risk underenforcement against facilitators and create arbitrary remedial gaps. By contrast, for the TVPA (a statute Congress enacted with specified defendants and remedies), courts should be more reluctant to imply additional forms of liability absent clear text, but that does not justify importing a categorical ban into the ATS’s limited, norm-by-norm framework.
